newsitem.title: INDIA: Hindu party plans no-trust vote against India PM.
newsitem.headline: Hindu party plans no-trust vote against India PM.

text.p: India's main opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) will seek a no-confidence vote against Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda in parliament next month, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported on Monday.

The agency quoted former BJP prime minister Atal Behari Vajpayee as saying in the northern town of Lucknow that he expects some deputies of the Congress party, Deve Gowda's reluctant make-or-break ally, to vote for the BJP's motion.

The BJP commands 195 votes in the 545-seat Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament). The Congress party, with 140 seats, is shoring up Deve Gowda's seven-month old government which has fewer than 200 deputies of its own.
PTI quoted Vajpayee as saying the BJP would encourage the Congress also to move a simultaneous no-confidence motion, saying: "The BJP will support such a motion if it is brought by the Congress."
Political analysts said earlier on Monday that the Congress did not appear ready to withdraw its support for Deve Gowda's United Front alliance in next month's budget session of parliament.
Indian media reports have said Deve Gowda and Congress party president Sitaram Kesri have been sending signals of mounting displeasure to each other over social invitations.
Last week Deve Gowda pointedly failed to attend a reception hosted by Kesri reception to mark the breaking of the daily fast during the Moslem month of Ramadan.
The next day's newspapers were plastered with articles saying Deve Gowda's absence reflected growing ill will between the leaders.

In a tit-for-tat gesture, Kesri, who took over leadership of Congress in September after the party suffered its worst ever showing in general elections, boycotted Deve Gowda's own "iftar" reception on Saturday evening.

The new Congress chief was questioned earlier this month by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), the federal police agency, in connection with public interest litigation accusing Kesri of amassing wealth disproportionate to his known income.

The interrogation sent a chill through the Congress camp, which interpreted the move as a signal from Deve Gowda to Kesri to keep his distance. But the prime minister said he had no control over the CBI's work.
Kesri, meanwhile, has quietly held talks with leaders of Deve Gowda's coalition partners, newspapers said.
Analysts said the manoeuvring reflected increased tension between the two men but may not lead to a showdown.

"I don't think Congress is at all keen to precipitate a crisis that would mean going back to elections which they don't want because they would do badly," said Ashis Nandy of the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies.
